faq.q: What part of the brain controls breathing?
faq.a: The brainstem, at the base of the brain, has a breathing centre that sets your breathing rate automatically. It responds mainly to carbon dioxide levels in the blood.
asks: Tell me about the brainstem noticing
What controls how fast we breathe?

faq.q: Why do you breathe faster when you run?
faq.a: Running muscles make more carbon dioxide and need more oxygen. Breathing faster and deeper removes the extra carbon dioxide and brings in more oxygen.
asks: Tell me about faster, deeper breaths

faq.q: Is it lack of oxygen that makes you breathe harder?
faq.a: Mostly no. In everyday exercise the strongest signal is rising carbon dioxide and acidity in the blood. Low oxygen only becomes a strong trigger in situations like high altitude.
asks: Does low oxygen make you pant?

faq.q: Why do you keep panting after you stop?
faq.a: Your body still has extra carbon dioxide to remove and needs extra oxygen to restore energy stores and clear the chemical changes in the muscles, so breathing settles down gradually.
asks: Why am I still out of breath after running?

faq.q: How much more air do you breathe in exercise?
faq.a: At rest an adult breathes about 6 litres of air a minute. During very hard exercise it can rise to over 100 litres a minute.
asks: How much air do lungs move during exercise?

facts: Rising carbon dioxide in the blood is the main everyday trigger for breathing more.
Breathing in an adult can rise from about 6 litres a minute at rest to over 100 litres a minute in hard exercise.
